targetAudience: PMs and engineers deciding how to build an LLM feature; product leaders reviewing 'agentic' proposals
topic: Agent vs workflow: the question that decides it
coreInsight: If you can draw the steps in advance, build a workflow and add AI only where judgment is needed; reserve agents for tasks whose steps can’t be known up front.

hookVariants.text: Your AI agent might just be a workflow in disguise.
Stop calling every LLM feature an agent.
One question decides: agent or workflow?

selectedHook: Your AI agent might just be a workflow in disguise.
selectionRationale: Highest total (23/25). It reframes a hyped label in plain words, sparks recognition in teams building ‘agents’, and the reel resolves it with a decision rule viewers can share with their team.

script.onScreen: WORKFLOW / You draw the steps. / Fixed steps, written in code · Predictable cost and latency · Easy to test and audit
script.voiceover: In a workflow, you draw the steps. They're fixed in code, cost and latency are predictable, and it's easy to test.

script.onScreen: AGENT / The model picks the steps. / Model chooses the next step · Cost varies per request · Needs trajectory evals
script.voiceover: In an agent, the model picks the steps. That buys flexibility, but cost varies per request and you have to evaluate the whole path, not just the answer.

script.onScreen: THE DECISION RULE / Use an agent only when… / steps unknowable · actions reversible or gated · flexibility worth variable cost · trajectory can be evaluated / Otherwise: build the workflow, add AI where judgment is needed.
script.voiceover: Use an agent only when the steps can't be known in advance, wrong actions are reversible or gated, the flexibility is worth variable cost, and you can evaluate the whole trajectory. Otherwise, build the workflow and add AI at the steps that need judgment.

caption:
If you can draw the steps on a whiteboard, you probably don’t need an agent.

Workflow: you define the steps; an LLM handles the parts that need judgment. Predictable, testable, cheaper to run.

Agent: the model decides the next step. More flexible, but cost varies per request and you have to evaluate the whole path it took, not just the final answer.

Use an agent only when:
→ the steps can’t be known in advance
→ wrong actions are reversible or need approval
→ the flexibility is worth variable cost
→ you can evaluate the trajectory

claims.text: If the steps of a task can be specified in advance, a workflow with LLM steps is usually more predictable and easier to test than an agent.
